title: Hip fracture pathway
subtitle: Analgesia now, theatre within a day, walk the next

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Hip fracture: management (CG124)

sources.org: Association of Anaesthetists (Griffiths R et al). Anaesthesia 76:225
sources.title: Guideline for the management of hip fractures 2020

sources.org: Baumgaertner MR et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am 77:1058
sources.title: The value of the tip-apex distance in predicting failure of fixation of peritrochanteric fractures of the hip

red_flags.text: A collapse rather than a trip: syncope, arrhythmia, stroke or sepsis may have caused the fall.
A long lie: rhabdomyolysis, pressure injury, hypothermia and acute kidney injury.
New confusion. Delirium is common, worsens outcome and is often missed when it is quiet.
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment: plan reversal or timing now, not on the morning of surgery.
Pain before the fall, a low-energy fracture in a non-osteoporotic patient, or known cancer: suspect a pathological fracture.
Normal radiographs in a patient who still cannot weight-bear: an occult fracture until imaging says otherwise.

do_now.text: Give immediate analgesia on arrival, including to people with cognitive impairment: regular paracetamol, opioids if needed, and a nerve block by trained staff if those are insufficient.
Assess pain on arrival, within 30 minutes of the first analgesia, and hourly until settled.

Identify and treat correctable problems immediately so they do not delay surgery: anaemia, anticoagulation, volume depletion, electrolytes, diabetes, heart failure, arrhythmia or ischaemia, and chest infection.
Look actively for cognitive impairment and delirium at presentation.

assess.text: Shortened, externally rotated leg; skin and pressure areas; distal neurovascular status.
Screen for delirium and cognition, and record pre-fracture mobility, residence and frailty.
Establish why she fell: ECG, lying and standing blood pressure when possible, and a medication review.
Anticoagulant: which agent, the last dose and renal function. This sets the earliest safe time for theatre.

investigate.text: Anteroposterior pelvis and lateral hip radiographs.
If radiographs are negative but suspicion persists, MRI; if MRI is not available within 24 hours or is contraindicated, consider CT.
Full blood count, renal function, electrolytes, group and save, ECG; creatine kinase after a long lie; coagulation when anticoagulated.
Do not let a test that will not change the anaesthetic plan delay surgery.

resuscitate.text: Correct volume depletion and electrolyte disturbance with intravenous fluids while awaiting theatre.
Offer a choice of spinal or general anaesthesia after discussion, and consider an intra-operative nerve block.

definitive.text: Operate on the day of, or the day after, admission, on a planned trauma list with senior supervision.
Operate so the patient can fully weight-bear without restriction immediately afterwards.

Displaced intracapsular fracture: replacement arthroplasty with cemented implants. Consider total hip replacement for those who walked outdoors with no more than a stick, are fit for it, and are expected to remain independent beyond 2 years.
Trochanteric fracture above and including the lesser trochanter, other than reverse oblique: sliding hip screw in preference to a nail.
With a sliding hip screw, place the lag screw centrally in the head with a small tip-apex distance; a large distance predicts cut-out.
Physiotherapy assessment and mobilisation on the day after surgery, within an orthogeriatric Hip Fracture Programme that starts at admission.

escalate.text: Orthogeriatric review from admission, not after the operation.
If the fracture complicates a terminal illness, surgery may still be the best palliation for pain. Make that decision with the patient and family.
Suspected pathological fracture: hold, image the whole bone, and discuss with the metastatic bone disease service before fixing.
Any delay beyond the next day: escalate the reason and who is resolving it.

notes: The Nottingham Hip Fracture Score is not in the calculator library. Use the frailty, cognition and delirium tools here and document the conversation about expected outcome.
Cemented hemiarthroplasty carries a risk of bone cement implantation syndrome. The team brief should name the high-risk patient and the plan before cement is mixed.
Undisplaced intracapsular fractures are usually fixed; in a frail patient some units prefer arthroplasty. Follow local policy and record the reasoning.
